Visual improvement was observed in 339 eyes (60.2%), stability in 122 eyes (21.7%), and deterioration in 102 eyes (18.1%) (Table 2). chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS soft­ ware (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Within-group comparisons of baseline and 12-month BCVA were performed using paired t-tests. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The association between injection number and visual acuity change was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Treatment switching Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept was considered in eyes demonstrating inadequate ana­ tomical or functional response. Inadequate response was defined as persistent retinal fluid, insufficient ana­ tomical improvement on OCT assessment, or lack of satisfactory functional improvement, as judged by the treating physician, despite repeated injections. Because of the retrospective real-world design, no rigid quanti­ tative anatomical or visual acuity thresholds were pre­ defined; treatment switching decisions were based on the treating physician's overall clinical judgment integrat­ ing both anatomical and functional response. For eyes undergoing treatment switching, the timing of switching, BCVA before switching, and BCVA after switching were recorded. Treatment switching was unidirectional from bevacizumab to aflibercept during the 12-month study period; no eyes switched back to bevacizumab or under­ went additional therapeutic modifications. Multivariable linear regression To identify independent predictors of visual outcomes, a multivariable linear regression analysis was per­ formed. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR). Independent variables included baseline BCVA, total number of injections during the first year, and treatment switching status. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and prior literature. Regres­ sion coefficients (β) and corresponding P values were reported. Generalized estimating equation analysis To account for potential inter-eye correlation arising from inclusion of both eyes from some patients, a gener­ alized estimating equation (GEE) model was performed using an exchangeable working correlation structure with robust standard errors. Patient identifier was specified as the clustering variable. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), and independent variables included baseline BCVA, number of injections, treat­ ment switching status, age, and sex. Data collection Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Variables included age, sex, number of outpatient visits, total number of intravitreal injections, baseline and 12-month BCVA, and treatment switching status. BCVA was measured using Snellen charts and converted to logarithm of the minimum angle of reso­ lution (logMAR) units using standardized conversion methods. Visual acuity change (ΔlogMAR) was calcu­ lated as the difference between 12-month and baseline values, with negative values indicating visual improve­ ment. Visual outcomes were additionally categorized as improvement (decrease in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR), sta­ bility (change in BCVA between - 0.1 and + 0.1 logMAR), or deterioration (increase in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR). Sensitivity analysis As a sensitivity analysis, the regression model was repeated after restricting the dataset to one randomly selected eye per patient to assess the robustness of the findings. For subgroup analysis, eyes were stratified according to the median baseline BCVA value (1.0 log­ MAR).

chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Hasan Öncül1*, Umut Dağ1, Hüseyin Dinç1 and Mehmet Fuat Alakuş1 Abstract Background To evaluate real-world injection burden, treatment switching patterns, and visual outcomes in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) receiving intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy. Materials and methods This retrospective observational cohort study included 563 eyes with DME treated with anti-VEGF agents and followed for at least 12 months. All eyes received an initial loading phase of three monthly bevacizumab injections followed by a pro re nata regimen. Primary outcomes were the number of injections and outpatient visits during the first year. Secondary outcomes included change in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), distribution of visual outcomes, and treatment switching patterns. Multivariable linear regression and generalized estimating equation (GEE) analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of visual outcomes. Results Eyes received a mean of 5.4 ± 2.4 injections and attended 8.0 ± 2.2 visits during the first year. Mean BCVA improved from 0.75 ± 0.43 to 0.59 ± 0.42 logMAR (mean change - 0.16 ± 0.35; P < 0.001). Visual improvement was observed in 60.2% of eyes, stability in 21.7%, and deterioration in 18.1%. Treatment switching occurred in 29.7% of eyes, typically within the first 4-5 months. In multivariable linear regression analysis, baseline BCVA was associated with visual acuity change (β = -0.33, P < 0.001). Treatment switching was associated with visual outcomes in unadjusted analysis but was not independently associated after adjustment. In the GEE analysis accounting for inter-eye correlation, baseline BCVA remained significantly associated with visual acuity change (P < 0.001), whereas injection number (P = 0.527) and treatment switching (P = 0.976) were not associated. Conclusions In real-world clinical practice, anti-VEGF therapy for DME was associated with meaningful visual improvement despite a moderate injection frequency. Visual outcomes were primarily associated with baseline visual acuity rather than treatment intensity. Treatment switching was not independently associated with visual acuity change after adjustment, suggesting that it likely reflects underlying disease refractoriness rather than acting as an independent factor associated with visual outcomes; however, causal inference cannot be established due to the observational study design. These findings underscore the importance of individualized treatment strategies in DME. chunks.document_content: Allocation Anti-VEGF combined with retinal laser photocoagulation ac-counted for 45.65% of the main combination regimens. Anti-VEGF drugs (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) rapidly reduce macular edema and inhibit neovascular activity by neutralizing VEGF, with a fast onset but limited duration of action. Laser photocoagulation, by contrast, destroys high oxygen-consuming photoreceptor cells to reduce retinal ischemia and hypoxia, thereby decreasing sustained VEGF production; it offers durable efficacy but a slower onset. Seminal trials, including the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) and DRCR.net Protocol I, have established the evidence base for current management strat-egies: ETDRS defined diagnostic criteria and laser standards, while Protocol I validated combination therapy efficacy. Anti-VEGF combined with glucocorticoids may benefit patients who respond poorly to anti-VEGF therapy alone, but the adverse effects such as increased intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression limit their widespread use. The current main treatment regimen for CI-DME/PDR is centered on anti-VEGF therapy, with individual-ized plans optimized based on patient-specific conditions. Future research should focus on optimizing combination regimen timing, identifying suitable patient populations, the exploration of novel combination strategies (34). The sample sizes of diabetic retinopathy studies are generally small - 61.81% enrolled fewer than 100 participants, with studies of 1-50 participants being the most common (39.18%), while large-scale trials with over 300 participants accounted for only 13.15%. This scarcity of adequately powered studies is partly attributable to the relatively small PDR patient pool at individual centers, making it difficult for single sites to accrue more than 100 cases (36). Small samples compromise statistical power and increase the risk of type II errors, thereby undermining both internal validity and reproduc-ibility of reported treatment effects. The establishment of multicen-ter collaborative networks, such as the DRCR.net series (Protocol I/ T/V), RESTORE, RESOLVE, and VISTA/VIVID, is therefore es-sential not only to increase enrollment capacity but also to ensure sufficient power for detecting clinically meaningful effects and to enhance the generalizability of findings across diverse populations (37). Future trials should prespecify minimum sample size calcula-tions based on clinically relevant effect sizes and incorporate interim power analyses where appropriate. Age standards are primarily focused on adults, consistent with normal research patterns. Gender standards did not impose restrictions, reflecting good awareness of external validity. Only one study was limited to males. Overall, reporting on the gender dimension is relatively standardized, but subsequent analyses should still pay attention to efficacy differences in gender subgroups. Baseline CRT values in women are usually lower than in men, which may affect the diagnostic threshold for DME and the assessment of treatment response. The United States demonstrated a strong emphasis on anti-VEGF therapies, with a total of 69 studies (47 trial registrations and 22 publications) indexed in PubMed. In contrast, China showed a predominant focus on perioperative interventions, with a total of 40 studies (35 trial registrations and 5 publications in PubMed). These findings suggest that geographical regions may have specific prior-ities in therapeutic strategies, accompanied by varying rates of translation from registration to publication. Intervention timing is mostly individualized, often without fixed treatment numbers and frequencies.

chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study ​Introduction Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of vision loss among individuals with diabetes mellitus and represents a major global health burden. The prevalence of DME continues to rise in parallel with the increasing incidence of diabetes worldwide, particularly in aging populations. Vision impairment due to DME significantly affects patients' quality of life and imposes substantial socioeconomic costs on healthcare systems [1, 2]. associated visual outcomes remains limited and hetero­ geneous [10, 11]. In addition, the treatment burden associated with repeated intravitreal injections and frequent clinical vis­ its represents a major challenge for both patients and healthcare systems. Understanding real-world injection patterns and their relationship with functional outcomes is therefore essential for optimizing long-term manage­ ment strategies in DME [9, 12]. The pathophysiology of DME is primarily driven by dis­ ruption of the blood-retinal barrier and increased vascu­ lar permeability mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Elevated intraocular VEGF levels lead to retinal thickening, fluid accumulation, and progres­ sive visual decline [3]. As a result, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy has become the first-line treatment for center-involving DME, largely replacing macular laser photoco­ agulation in routine clinical practice [4]. Given these considerations, real-world data derived from large clinical cohorts are essential to complement findings from randomized trials and to better reflect rou­ tine clinical practice. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to evaluate real-world injection burden, treat­ ment switching patterns, and visual outcomes in a large cohort of patients with DME treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy. Specifically, we sought to determine whether visual outcomes are more strongly associated with treatment intensity or baseline visual acuity. The efficacy of anti-VEGF therapy in DME has been firmly established in multiple randomized controlled trials. The RISE and RIDE studies demonstrated sig­ nificant and sustained visual acuity improvements with ranibizumab compared with sham injections [5], while the VIVID and VISTA trials confirmed the superiority of aflibercept over laser photocoagulation [6]. Further­ more, the DRCR.net Protocol T study showed that treat­ ment response varies according to baseline visual acuity, highlighting the importance of individualized therapeutic approaches [7]. These landmark trials have established anti-VEGF therapy as the standard of care for DME. Despite these favorable outcomes under controlled trial conditions, treatment patterns in real-world clinical practice often differ substantially from protocol-driven regimens. Real-world studies consistently report lower injection frequencies, irregular follow-up intervals, and heterogeneous retreatment strategies compared with randomized trials [8, 9]. Consequently, visual outcomes achieved in routine practice may be less pronounced than those reported in clinical trials, reflecting a gap between efficacy and effectiveness. In real-world clinical practice, additional challenges such as variability in patient adher­ ence, irregular follow-up intervals, differences in retreat­ ment criteria, and healthcare system constraints may further contribute to heterogeneity in treatment delivery and outcomes. Study population Eyes with a diagnosis of diabetic macular edema (DME), a minimum follow-up duration of 12 months, and no prior treatment for DME were included in the analysis. Eyes that had previously received anti-VEGF therapy, intravitreal corticosteroid treatment, or focal/grid laser photocoagulation for DME were excluded.

The diagno­ sis of DME was based on clinical examination and opti­ cal coherence tomography (OCT) findings. Eyes were excluded if baseline best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) data were unavailable or if significant ocular comorbidi­ ties that could affect visual acuity were present, including advanced glaucoma, dense cataract, or corneal opacity. Both eyes from the same patient were included if they met the eligibility criteria, reflecting routine clinical practice. Treatment switching represents another important aspect of DME management in real-world settings. A considerable proportion of patients exhibit subopti­ mal anatomical or functional response to initial anti-VEGF therapy, necessitating a switch to alternative agents. Although previous studies suggest that switch­ ing may provide additional benefit in selected cases, evi­ dence regarding optimal timing, patient selection, and Treatment protocol All eyes initially received three consecutive monthly intravitreal injections of bevacizumab as a loading phase, in accordance with institutional treatment protocols and reimbursement policies. Following the loading phase, patients were managed using a pro re nata (PRN) regi­ men. Retreatment decisions were based on OCT find­ ings and functional assessment. Criteria for retreatment included the presence of persistent or recurrent intra­ retinal or subretinal fluid, increased central macular thickness, or deterioration in BCVA compared with the previous visit. Patients were followed at monthly inter­ vals, during which OCT imaging was performed to guide retreatment decisions. and timing; and the association between injection num­ ber and visual acuity change.

Real-world data, such as those presented in this study, are essential for evaluating how these strategies may be implemented in clinical practice. The difference between the conventional multivariable regression and the GEE analysis is likely attributable to their differing underlying statistical assumptions. Con­ ventional regression assumes that each eye represents an independent observation, whereas the GEE model accounts for the within-patient correlation arising from the inclusion of both eyes from some patients. Failure to account for this correlation may underestimate standard errors, thereby increasing the likelihood of statistically significant findings. Because our study included bilateral observations, the GEE model was considered to provide the more appropriate population-averaged estimates and was therefore regarded as the primary inferential analysis. The strengths of this study include the large sample size and the comprehensive evaluation of treatment bur­ den, switching patterns, and visual outcomes within a single real-world clinical setting. In addition, the use of advanced statistical methods, including GEE analysis and sensitivity analysis restricted to one eye per patient, allowed for more robust estimation of treatment effects by accounting for inter-eye correlation and potential sources of bias. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective design limits causal inference and may introduce selection bias. Second, treatment decisions were not standardized and were made at the discretion of treating physicians, which may have influenced treat­ ment patterns and outcomes. In particular, treatment switching is subject to confounding by indication, as it is preferentially applied to eyes with inadequate response. This limits the ability to disentangle its independent effect on visual outcomes. Although inter-eye correla­ tion was addressed using generalized estimating equation analysis, residual correlation and unmeasured confound­ ing cannot be completely excluded. This may include unmeasured differences in patient demographics, sys­ temic comorbidities, and disease-related characteristics that could influence both treatment patterns and visual outcomes. Residual confounding inherent to the obser­ vational nature of the study cannot be fully ruled out, particularly with respect to treatment switching, which may reflect underlying disease severity and physician decision-making. The timing of treatment switching was not modeled as a time-dependent variable, which may have influenced the observed associations. Furthermore, important systemic factors such as duration of diabe­ tes, glycemic control, and other vascular comorbidities were not included in the analysis. The severity stage of diabetic retinopathy (e.g., non-proliferative versus pro­ liferative diabetic retinopathy) was also not consistently available in the retrospective records and therefore could not be incorporated into the analysis.

chunks.document_content: oversightModule oversightHasDmc: False detailedDescription: Panretinal photocoagulation can cause regression of retinal neovascularization and reduce the risk of severe vision loss in people with proliferative diabetic retinopathy. However, this destructive treatment may be associated with side effects (such as: pain, transient blurring, loss of peripheral and/or night vision, increased risk of macular edema and central vision loss) and it is not always efficient in the regression of the neovascularization. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) has been shown to play a role in retinal neovascularization and retinal vascular leakage related with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor treatments have been hypothesized as an alternative adjunctive treatment for the management of retinal neovascularization and macular edema related with diabetic retinopathy. There are a few reports of retinal traction detachment in patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and fibrovascular proliferation (although it is not frequent). However, from our clinical experience, we think that the risk of detachment only exists when there is in place a fibrovascular proliferation with retinal traction previous to the injection. We injected ranibizumab prior to surgery in patients with severe proliferative diabetic retinopathy, that were submitted later to a posterior vitrectomy, to reduce neovascularization and minimize the risk of an intraoperatory hemorrhage caused by the manipulation of the fibrovascular membranes. In total, we already injected and submitted to surgery 15 eyes with the above mentioned condition, with excellent results. The results of the first 10 eyes were presented in the congress of the Portuguese Society of Ophthalmology (2008).
